evidence_quotes.quote: The analysis reveals that rate regulation, intended to make water service affordable to all households, is also responsible, and may actually reduce service coverage among the poor.
None of these public provider types can charge different water rates to different residential customers, based on cost of service.
The infrastructure-related data used in this study come from the TWDB Colonias Database.
I use a probit model to examine the relationship between a colonia's likelihood of receipt of water service by 1996 (the dependent variable) and the independent variables.
Thus, relying on a price-regulated supplier to provide service reduces the likelihood of having obtained service through 1996 by 27%.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level central drinking water service coverage and acquisition across unincorporated settlements (colonias) in four Texas border counties.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines regulatory, institutional, and governance determinants of water service provision (rate regulation by municipalities and TCEQ, utility ownership/institutional form, and county subdivision regulation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly tests rule-type mechanisms governing service access: tariff and cost-recovery rules (price regulation vs. pricing flexibility to charge cost-based capital recovery fees and rates in the absence of a statutory universal service mandate within Certificates of Convenience and Necessity), utility ownership and regulatory structure (municipalities, counties/general law water districts, non-profit water supply corporations, and for-profit private providers), and regulatory enforcement (county citations for lax enforcement of Model Subdivision Rules conditioning state infrastructure subsidy eligibility).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative econometric analysis (probit regression models A and B and difference-in-means/proportions tests) of 781 colonias using merged administrative and demographic datasets from the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) Colonias Database and the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) Texas Border Database.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports an explicit service access outcome: whether a colonia had obtained central drinking water utility service coverage by 1996 (binary variable water96).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and settlement-level unit of analysis (781 colonias in Cameron, El Paso, Hidalgo, and Webb counties, Texas), the legal/regulatory exposures (rate regulation, provider institutional type, subsidy eligibility, and county MSR adoption/enforcement), the access outcome (water service coverage by 1996), and the study design (cross-sectional probit regression). Statistical information (coefficients, robust clustered standard errors, p-values, marginal effects, n = 781) is also fully reported.

population_and_sample: Unincorporated residential settlements (colonias) in four Texas border counties (Cameron, El Paso, Hidalgo, and Webb); settlement-level unit of analysis, n = 781 colonias (ranging from 4 to 5,200 residents, mean population 264).
exposure: Water rate/tariff regulation (price-regulated municipal, county, and water district suppliers vs. unregulated non-profit water supply corporations and for-profit suppliers in the absence of a universal service mandate), utility ownership/institutional type, provider eligibility for USDA Rural Development subsidies, and county adoption timing and enforcement violations of Model Subdivision Rules (MSR).
outcome: Central drinking water service coverage by 1996 (binary settlement-level indicator water96).
rationale: Full-text empirical econometric study examining how tariff/rate regulation, utility ownership and regulatory structure (under Texas CCN territorial rules without universal service mandates), subsidy eligibility rules, and county enforcement of Model Subdivision Rules affect central drinking water service coverage across 781 Texas border colonias. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2.
